items.stem: Which of the following best describes "intensive farming"?
options: Combining arable and pastoral farming on the same farm
Growing crops such as wheat, rice or maize
When a person's regular food intake is not enough to provide the energy needed for a healthy, active life
Farming with high inputs of labour or capital per hectare to achieve high yields
items.answer: Farming with high inputs of labour or capital per hectare to achieve high yields
items.markingKey: D. "intensive farming" is farming with high inputs of labour or capital per hectare to achieve high yields.

items.stem: A student claims: "Subsistence farming is always extensive." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Wet-rice farming in South and East Asia is intensive subsistence farming with very high labour inputs.
items.markingKey: Wet-rice farming in South and East Asia is intensive subsistence farming with very high labour inputs. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between subsistence farming and commercial farming.
items.answer: Subsistence farming produces food mainly for the family; commercial farming produces for sale and profit.
items.markingKey: Subsistence farming produces food mainly for the family; commercial farming produces for sale and profit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "What is farming?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into farming systems: subsistence and commercial, arable and pastoral. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a definition question Improved: "How has the size of soybean farms in Mato Grosso, Brazil, changed between 2000 and 2020, and why?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a definition question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How has the size of soybean farms in Mato Grosso, Brazil, changed between 2000 and 2020, and why?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why physical factors influence the type of farming in an area.
items.answer: Climate, relief and soil determine what can grow: steep, dry or cold land suits pastoral farming, while flat, fertile, well-watered land suits arable farming.
items.markingKey: Content: Climate, relief and soil determine what can grow: steep, dry or cold land suits pastoral farming, while flat, fertile, well-watered land suits arable farming. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How has the size of soybean farms in Mato Grosso, Brazil, changed between 2000 and 2020, and why?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Use IBGE agricultural census data, satellite images and two studies; graph change; explain factors; evaluate sources; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use IBGE agricultural census data, satellite images and two studies; graph change; explain factors; evaluate sources; cite in APA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "subsistence farming".
items.answer: Farming to produce food mainly for the farmer's own family, with little surplus to sell
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: farming to produce food mainly for the farmer's own family, with little surplus to sell. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why farming is often described as a system.
items.answer: A farm has inputs (land, labour, seeds, fertiliser, machinery), processes (ploughing, sowing, harvesting) and outputs (crops, animals, waste), with feedback such as profits reinvested.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A farm has inputs (land, labour, seeds, fertiliser, machinery), processes (ploughing, sowing, harvesting) and outputs (crops, animals, waste), with feedback such as profits reinvested. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between intensive farming and extensive farming.
items.answer: Intensive farming uses high inputs on small areas for high yields per hectare; extensive farming uses low inputs over large areas with lower yields per hectare.
items.markingKey: Intensive farming uses high inputs on small areas for high yields per hectare; extensive farming uses low inputs over large areas with lower yields per hectare. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source A – FAO report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, The State of Food and Agriculture 2014

The report estimated that there are about 608 million family farms in the world, operating around 70–80% of farmland and producing about 80% of the world's food in value terms. It noted that most are very small, with less than two hectares.

Outline the main argument or view that Source A presents, quoting or referring to the source.
items.answer: Small family farms produce most of the world's food.
items.markingKey: Small family farms produce most of the world's food. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into farming systems: subsistence and commercial, arable and pastoral?
options: How has the size of soybean farms in Mato Grosso, Brazil, changed between 2000 and 2020, and why?
items.answer: How has the size of soybean farms in Mato Grosso, Brazil, changed between 2000 and 2020, and why?
items.markingKey: C. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Commercial farming is better than subsistence farming for developing countries." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Commercial farming can drive growth, but a mix is often best, supporting smallholders to raise productivity and sell surpluses while protecting food security.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it raises incomes, exports and productivity; it can provide jobs and foreign currency. Counter-arguments: it can increase inequality, land concentration and environmental damage; subsistence farming supports food security and resilience for millions of families. Thesis/conclusion: Commercial farming can drive growth, but a mix is often best, supporting smallholders to raise productivity and sell surpluses while protecting food security. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "high-yielding variety (HYV)".
items.answer: A crop variety bred to produce much larger harvests, such as dwarf wheat and IR8 rice
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a crop variety bred to produce much larger harvests, such as dwarf wheat and IR8 rice. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "The Green Revolution ended hunger in India." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It made India self-sufficient in grain, but malnutrition remains widespread because of poverty and unequal access to food.
items.markingKey: It made India self-sufficient in grain, but malnutrition remains widespread because of poverty and unequal access to food. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between traditional crop varieties and high-yielding varieties.
items.answer: Traditional varieties are hardier and need fewer inputs but yield less; HYVs give much higher yields but require irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides.
items.markingKey: Traditional varieties are hardier and need fewer inputs but yield less; HYVs give much higher yields but require irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "The Green Revolution was a success for India." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: It succeeded in its main aim of food self-sufficiency, but its social and environmental costs mean its success was partial and its model needs reform.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: wheat and rice production soared and India became self-sufficient in grain; it reduced the risk of famine and dependence on food aid. Counter-arguments: benefits were unequal and many farmers fell into debt; it caused groundwater depletion, soil degradation and pollution. Thesis/conclusion: It succeeded in its main aim of food self-sufficiency, but its social and environmental costs mean its success was partial and its model needs reform. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

The speaker argued that the Green Revolution had won a temporary success in the war against hunger and had given humanity breathing space. He warned that unless the growth of population was brought under control, the gains would be only temporary.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "The Green Revolution was a success for India."
items.answer: It succeeded in its main aim of food self-sufficiency, but its social and environmental costs mean its success was partial and its model needs reform.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Green Revolution"?
options: India's system of selling subsidised food grains through ration shops
The rapid increase in crop yields from the 1960s using high-yielding varieties, irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides
The Indian geneticist who led the introduction of HYV wheat in India in the 1960s
The US agronomist who developed dwarf wheat varieties in Mexico and won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize
items.answer: The rapid increase in crop yields from the 1960s using high-yielding varieties, irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides
items.markingKey: B. "Green Revolution" is the rapid increase in crop yields from the 1960s using high-yielding varieties, irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the Green Revolution caused environmental problems.
items.answer: Heavy use of fertilisers and pesticides polluted soils and water, monoculture reduced biodiversity, and tube-well irrigation lowered water tables and caused salinisation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Heavy use of fertilisers and pesticides polluted soils and water, monoculture reduced biodiversity, and tube-well irrigation lowered water tables and caused salinisation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ana writes: "The Green Revolution increased production of all crops." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It mainly increased wheat and rice; pulses and coarse grains grew more slowly, and their share of farmland fell.
items.markingKey: It mainly increased wheat and rice; pulses and coarse grains grew more slowly, and their share of farmland fell. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

The speaker argued that the Green Revolution had won a temporary success in the war against hunger and had given humanity breathing space. He warned that unless the growth of population was brought under control, the gains would be only temporary.

According to Source A, what can we learn about the Green Revolution in India: its causes, benefits and problems? Support your answer with details from the source.
items.answer: The Green Revolution bought time against hunger, but population growth remained a challenge.
items.markingKey: The Green Revolution bought time against hunger, but population growth remained a challenge. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why the benefits of the Green Revolution were unequal.
items.answer: HYVs needed irrigation, fertilisers and credit, so richer farmers in irrigated areas such as Punjab gained most, while poorer farmers and dry regions benefited less.
items.markingKey: Content: HYVs needed irrigation, fertilisers and credit, so richer farmers in irrigated areas such as Punjab gained most, while poorer farmers and dry regions benefited less. items.stem: The data show India's food-grain production (Government of India, approx.): 1950: 51 million tonnes; 1970: 108 million tonnes; 1990: 176 million tonnes; 2010: 218 million tonnes; 2023: 330 million tonnes. Calculate the average rate of change per year between 1970 and 2023, and use the data to describe whether the change is speeding up or slowing down.
items.answer: +4.19 million tonnes per year (+41.9 per decade); speeding up
items.markingKey: (330 − 108) ÷ (2023 − 1970) = +4.19 million tonnes/year (M1 A1); × 10 = +41.9 per decade (A1). Earliest interval +2.85/yr vs latest +8.62/yr → speeding up (R2, data quoted).

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How has the Green Revolution affected groundwater levels in Punjab between 1970 and 2020?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Use Central Ground Water Board data and two studies; graph water-table change; compare districts; evaluate sources; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use Central Ground Water Board data and two studies; graph water-table change; compare districts; evaluate sources; cite in APA. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "food security".
items.answer: When all people at all times have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food (FAO, 1996)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: when all people at all times have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food (FAO, 1996). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between food availability and food access.
items.answer: Availability is whether enough food is produced or imported; access is whether people can afford or otherwise obtain it.
items.markingKey: Availability is whether enough food is produced or imported; access is whether people can afford or otherwise obtain it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why food waste is relevant to food security.
items.answer: About a third of food is lost or wasted globally; reducing waste would increase the food available without using more land or water. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: About a third of food is lost or wasted globally; reducing waste would increase the food available without using more land or water. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A class brainstorm on food security and food insecurity: causes and solutions produced the question "Why are people hungry?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.
items.answer: Weakness: it is too broad and has no focus Improved: "How effective has India's Public Distribution System been in reducing food insecurity in Odisha since 2013?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is too broad and has no focus); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How effective has India's Public Distribution System been in reducing food insecurity in Odisha since 2013?" Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: "Hunger is only a problem in poor countries." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Food insecurity also affects people in rich countries; millions use food banks in the UK and the US.
items.markingKey: Food insecurity also affects people in rich countries; millions use food banks in the UK and the US. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Poverty, rather than food shortage, is the main cause of food insecurity today."
items.answer: Poverty and access are the main causes globally, but conflict and climate shocks create real shortages; solutions must address both access and supply.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the world produces enough calories for everyone; Sen showed famines often occur when food is available but unaffordable. Arguments against: in conflict zones and droughts, local food shortages are real; climate change is reducing yields in vulnerable regions. Supported judgement: Poverty and access are the main causes globally, but conflict and climate shocks create real shortages; solutions must address both access and supply.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "When a person's regular food intake is not enough to provide the energy needed for a healthy, active life"?
items.answer: undernourishment
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of undernourishment.

items.stem: Explain why conflict is a major cause of food insecurity.
items.answer: Fighting disrupts farming, destroys markets and infrastructure, displaces people and blocks aid, as in Sudan, Yemen and Gaza.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Fighting disrupts farming, destroys markets and infrastructure, displaces people and blocks aid, as in Sudan, Yemen and Gaza. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between chronic food insecurity and acute food insecurity.
items.answer: Chronic food insecurity is long-term inability to meet food needs; acute food insecurity is a sudden, severe shortage caused by shocks such as drought or war.
items.markingKey: Chronic food insecurity is long-term inability to meet food needs; acute food insecurity is a sudden, severe shortage caused by shocks such as drought or war. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source A – UN report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of FAO, IFAD, UNICEF, WFP and WHO, The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2024

The report found that around 733 million people faced hunger in 2023, about one in eleven people worldwide and one in five in Africa. It concluded that the world was far off track to meet the goal of zero hunger by 2030 and identified conflict, climate extremes and economic downturns as the main drivers.

With reference to its origin and purpose, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for a student investigating food security and food insecurity: causes and solutions.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of FAO, IFAD, UNICEF, WFP and WHO, The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2024. Purpose: to monitor progress towards SDG 2 and inform policy. Value: It is produced jointly by five UN agencies using global survey data. Limitation: Hunger estimates are modelled and less certain in conflict zones; it summarises global trends rather than local experience.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of FAO, IFAD, UNICEF, WFP and WHO, The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2024. Purpose: to monitor progress towards SDG 2 and inform policy. Value: It is produced jointly by five UN agencies using global survey data. Limitation: Hunger estimates are modelled and less certain in conflict zones; it summarises global trends rather than local experience. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". items.stem: Which crop is typically grown on large commercial plantations in Assam?
items.answer: Tea

items.stem: Which economist won the Nobel Prize partly for showing that the 1943 Bengal famine occurred without a major fall in food supply?
items.answer: Amartya Sen

items.stem: Explain the difference between the benefits of the Green Revolution and the problems of the Green Revolution.
items.answer: Benefits include food self-sufficiency and higher incomes; problems include inequality, debt, water depletion, soil degradation and loss of crop diversity.

items.stem: A student claims: "Pastoral farming always means nomadic herding." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Pastoral farming includes settled dairy and beef farms as well as nomadic herding.
items.markingKey: Pastoral farming includes settled dairy and beef farms as well as nomadic herding. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Data from approx., Government of India: India's food-grain production – 1966: 74 million tonnes; 2000: 197 million tonnes. By what percentage did it change over the period? Show your working.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Commercial farming is better than subsistence farming for developing countries."
items.answer: Commercial farming can drive growth, but a mix is often best, supporting smallholders to raise productivity and sell surpluses while protecting food security.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it raises incomes, exports and productivity; it can provide jobs and foreign currency. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The Green Revolution was a success for India."
items.answer: It succeeded in its main aim of food self-sufficiency, but its social and environmental costs mean its success was partial and its model needs reform.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: wheat and rice production soared and India became self-sufficient in grain; it reduced the risk of famine and dependence on food aid. Arguments against: benefits were unequal and many farmers fell into debt; it caused groundwater depletion, soil degradation and pollution. Supported judgement: It succeeded in its main aim of food self-sufficiency, but its social and environmental costs mean its success was partial and its model needs reform. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "famine"?

Farming to produce food mainly for the farmer's own family, with little surplus to sell
India's system of selling subsidised food grains through ration shops

items.stem: Distinguish between the benefits of the Green Revolution and the problems of the Green Revolution.
items.answer: Benefits include food self-sufficiency and higher incomes; problems include inequality, debt, water depletion, soil degradation and loss of crop diversity.

items.stem: Explain the difference between food access and food availability.
items.answer: Availability is whether enough food is produced or imported; access is whether people can afford or otherwise obtain it.
